text: How does a database find one row out of ten million almost instantly? It uses an index. A database index works like the index at the back of a textbook: you look up the topic and go straight to the right page instead of reading every page until you find it. Most indexes are built on a B-tree, which makes lookups O(log n). In practice, doubling the amount of data adds only one more step to a search instead of doubling the work. The difference can be large. In one real case, a query on a 10M-row table went from 2.1 seconds to 4 milliseconds, and users notice a change like that. Indexes do have a cost. They can slow writes by about 15%, because the database has to update the index on every insert and update. Below we'll look at how indexes work, when they help, and how to get faster reads without paying too much on writes.
